chapter_note.about: A Turing machine adds an unbounded tape to a finite control and defines the most general notion of computation. This chapter starts with tracing a machine and the models that have the same power, then separates recursive (decidable) languages from RE (recognisable) ones. It continues with the halting problem and the diagonal argument, Rice's theorem for properties of the language, reductions and how they transfer hardness, countability, and the bounded questions that stay decidable. Most questions ask you to classify a problem as decidable, RE or neither.
chapter_note.simple: A Turing machine is a little robot walking along an endless strip of paper, reading, writing and moving by a rule book. It is the most general kind of computer we know. Some questions about what robots do can be answered by a program that always finishes, and some cannot, however clever you are. The proof uses a robot that asks about itself and then does the opposite. Once you have one impossible question, you can show many others are impossible by turning the first into them. In exam words: Turing machines, recursive versus RE, halting, Rice's theorem, reductions, countability and bounded versions.

concept_map.title: Turing machine steps

concept_map.title: Equivalent models

concept_map.title: Halting and undecidable problems
concept_map.one_line: Halting, acceptance, emptiness and equality of TMs are undecidable; the halting language is RE and its complement is not.

concept_map.title: Rice's theorem
concept_map.one_line: Every non-trivial property of L(M) is undecidable; properties of M's description are not covered.

concept_map.title: Reductions
concept_map.one_line: A ≤m B passes decidability and RE-ness back from B to A, and undecidability and non-RE-ness forward from A to B.

concept_map.title: Countability
concept_map.one_line: Machines are countable, languages uncountable, so non-RE languages exist.

concept_map.title: Bounded versions
concept_map.one_line: A step bound makes a question decidable by simulation, even 'for all inputs', because only a bounded prefix matters.

cards.title: Turing machine steps
cards.simple: A Turing machine is a tiny robot walking along a long strip of paper. At each step it looks at the symbol it is standing on, and a rule book tells it three things: what to write there, whether to take one step left or right, and which mood (state) to switch to. It keeps going until it reaches a special 'finish' mood or until the rule book has no rule for what it sees. Tracing one by hand means writing down the strip, where the robot is, and its mood after every step. In exam words: a TM transition reads the symbol under the head, writes a symbol, moves the head L or R, and changes state; to trace it, tabulate state, head position and tape.
cards.idea: A **Turing machine** has a finite control, an unbounded tape and a head. Each **transition** reads the symbol under the head, **writes** a symbol, **moves** left or right, and **changes state**. It halts when it reaches an accepting or rejecting state, or when no transition applies. To trace one, keep a table of state, head position and tape.
cards.definition:
A deterministic TM is (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, B, F). The transition δ(q, a) = (p, b, D) means: in state q reading a, go to p, write b, move D ∈ {L, R}. B is the blank symbol and F the accepting states.

A configuration is (state, head position, tape contents). The machine halts when it enters a state in F or when δ(q, a) is undefined. It accepts if it halts in F, rejects if it halts elsewhere, and loops if it never halts. If the same configuration repeats, the machine loops forever.
cards.intuition_full: The tape is the memory and the head is a moving cursor, so an algorithm becomes a walk: scan right to find something, change it, come back. Unary arithmetic is a good example because the tape content is the number. Add 2 and 3 by turning + into 1 and erasing one 1 at the end. When tracing, always write the whole tape after each step, mark the head, and do not skip steps that only move the head. A machine can reject by halting in a non-accepting state or by running out of rules, and it can also loop. A repeated configuration, with the same state, head position and tape, is the proof of an infinite loop.

examples.setup: A TM has states q0, q1, q2, qa (accepting) and these transitions: q0 on 1 → (q0, 1, R); q0 on + → (q1, 1, R); q1 on 1 → (q1, 1, R); q1 on B → (q2, B, L); q2 on 1 → (qa, B, R). Trace it on the input 11+111 and count the transitions.
steps: A TM adds in unary: the input 11+111 stands for 2 + 3. Each transition reads the symbol under the head, writes a symbol, moves left or right, and changes state. The table gives every transition as (new state, symbol written, move). Start in q0 on the first cell.
q0 reads 1, writes 1, moves right, and does this twice. The head is now on the plus sign.
q0 reads +, writes 1 over it, moves right and goes to q1. The tape now reads 111111.
q1 reads 1 and moves right, three times, until it stands on the first blank.
q1 reads the blank, writes a blank, moves left and goes to q2.
q2 reads 1, writes a blank to erase the extra 1, moves right and goes to qa, the accepting state. The machine halts.
The tape holds 11111, five 1's, so 2 + 3 = 5. The run took 8 transitions: 3 in q0, 4 in q1 and 1 in q2.
examples.answer: It halts in qa after 8 transitions with 11111 on the tape (2 + 3 = 5).

examples.setup: A TM has the transitions q0 on 0 → (q1, 0, R) and q1 on 0 → (q0, 0, L), and no others. Does it halt on the input 0? On the input 00?
steps: Input 0: q0 reads 0, moves right and goes to q1. q1 reads the blank B. There is no transition for (q1, B), so the machine halts, and it rejects because q1 is not accepting.
Input 00: q0 reads 0, moves right to q1. q1 reads the second 0, moves left to q0. The head is back on cell 0 in q0 with the tape 00.
That configuration occurred at the start, so the machine will repeat the same two moves forever.
So it halts on 0 (rejecting) and loops on 00. A machine that loops on some strings recognises its language but does not decide it.
examples.answer: It halts on 0, rejecting, and loops forever on 00.

examples.setup: How many transitions does the same unary adder take on 4 + 2, written 1111+11?
steps: In q0: one transition for each 1 of the first number, plus one for the plus sign: 4 + 1 = 5.
In q1: one for each 1 of the second number, plus one for the blank: 2 + 1 = 3.
In q2: one transition to erase the last 1. Total 5 + 3 + 1 = 9, which is a + b + 3 in general. A simulation of the machine for a, b up to 6 agrees.
examples.answer: 9 transitions.

cards.title: Equivalent models
cards.simple: Imagine giving a robot extra strips of paper, extra arms, or the ability to try several things at once. It feels like it must become more powerful, but it does not. Anything the fancy robot can work out, the plain robot with one strip can work out too, just more slowly, by keeping everything on one strip and walking back and forth. For the 'try several things at once' version, the plain robot just tries the options one after another. So all these versions can solve exactly the same problems. In exam words: multi-tape, non-deterministic and two-way tape Turing machines accept the same languages as a standard single-tape deterministic TM.
cards.idea: Many variations of the Turing machine have **the same power**: several tapes, a non-deterministic choice of moves, a tape infinite in both directions, or a finite number of extra tracks. A single-tape deterministic machine can simulate each of them. Only the **time** changes, never which languages are accepted.
cards.intuition_full: The key idea in each simulation is to store the extra structure inside the one tape and pay with time. Several tapes become one tape with markers, and each simulated move needs a sweep. A non-deterministic machine's choices form a tree of configurations, and a deterministic machine can explore it level by level until an accepting branch appears. This is slow, possibly exponential, but it is still a computation. Two stacks are as strong as a tape: one stack holds the part left of the head and the other the part to the right. A single stack is weaker, because it cannot move both ways.

examples.setup: A 2-tape TM makes one move: it reads (b, 1), writes (x, 0) and moves both heads right. Tape 1 is abb with the head on the second cell, tape 2 is 10 with the head on the first cell. Show how a single-tape machine simulates the move.
steps: A 2-tape machine has two tapes and two heads. In one move it reads both cells, writes both, and moves both heads. Here it reads (b, 1), writes (x, 0) and moves both heads right.
A single-tape machine can simulate it. Write both tapes on one tape, separated by # signs.
Mark the cell under each head with a star: b* on tape 1 and 1* on tape 2. The stars are the heads.
To simulate the move, sweep the tape to find both starred cells and check they read (b, 1). Sweep again to apply the move: b becomes x, 1 becomes 0, and each star moves one cell right.
Each simulated move costs a sweep over the whole tape, so t moves of the 2-tape machine take at most about t² steps. This is slower, but it accepts exactly the same languages.
A non-deterministic TM is simulated by trying all branches one after another, breadth first, and a two-way infinite tape by folding it. None of these adds power, only speed.
examples.answer: Encode as #ab*b#1*0#. After the move the single tape is #axb*#00*#, which matches the two tapes axb (head on cell 3) and 00 (head on cell 2).

examples.setup: Which of these accept exactly the same languages as a deterministic single-tape TM? (i) a 3-tape TM  (ii) a non-deterministic TM  (iii) a PDA with two stacks  (iv) a PDA with one stack  (v) a linear bounded automaton
steps: (i) Simulate three tapes on one with separators and head marks: equivalent.
(ii) Search the tree of configurations breadth first: equivalent.
(iii) One stack holds the tape to the left of the head, the other the tape to the right. Moving the head moves a symbol from one stack to the other: equivalent.
(iv) One stack accepts only context-free languages, so it is weaker. (v) A linear bounded automaton accepts only context-sensitive languages, which are decidable, so it is weaker too.
examples.answer: (i), (ii) and (iii) are equivalent. (iv) and (v) are strictly weaker.

examples.setup: N is a non-deterministic TM that halts on every branch for every input (a non-deterministic decider). Is the language decidable by a deterministic TM?
steps: Simulate N by a breadth-first search over its tree of configurations.
Every branch is finite and every configuration has finitely many successors, so the whole tree is finite (König's lemma).
So the search ends: accept if some branch accepted, reject if the whole tree was explored without accepting.
examples.answer: Yes. A non-deterministic decider can be replaced by a deterministic decider, so the language is recursive.

cards.why: These equivalences show that the class of Turing-computable languages does not depend on the model chosen, and exam questions test it with 'which models are equivalent' lists. In GATE: pick the models with the same power as a TM, or state what changes (only time).
how: For a model with extra structure, ask how to store it on one tape.
For non-determinism, ask whether a breadth-first search over configurations works.
Remember the weaker models: finite automata, one-stack PDA, linear bounded automata.
Equivalence never means equal speed.
cards.mistake: Assuming a non-deterministic machine accepts more languages than a deterministic one (it does for PDAs, but not for TMs), or that a multi-tape machine is stronger. They are only faster. The opposite slip is to treat a linear bounded automaton as equal to a TM.
edge_cases: Non-determinism changes the running time, possibly from exponential to polynomial, but never the set of accepted languages.
A TM with a tape infinite in only one direction is still equivalent to a two-way one.
A TM with only one counter is weaker, two counters are as strong as a TM.
connections: Recursive versus RE (next card) holds for every one of these models.
The hierarchy card places TMs above linear bounded automata.

check.q: Does a 5-tape TM accept more languages than a 1-tape TM?
check.a: No. It accepts the same languages, only faster.

check.q: How does a deterministic TM simulate a non-deterministic one?
check.a: It explores all branches breadth first, level by level.

check.q: Is a PDA with two stacks as powerful as a TM?
check.a: Yes. The two stacks hold the tape left and right of the head.

cards.title: Recursive versus RE
cards.simple: There are two kinds of helpers. A decider always comes back with a yes or a no. A recogniser comes back with a yes if the answer is yes, but if the answer is no it might just keep working forever and never tell you. If you have one recogniser for 'yes' answers and another for 'no' answers, you can hire both and let them work in turns, one step each. One of them is guaranteed to finish, and as soon as one does you have your answer. In exam words: recursive means decided by a TM that always halts; RE means accepted by a TM that may loop on non-members; if both L and its complement are RE, then L is recursive.
cards.idea: A language is **recursive** (decidable) if a TM halts on every input and says yes or no. It is **recursively enumerable** (RE) if a TM halts and accepts exactly the members, but may loop on non-members. Every recursive language is RE. If **both L and its complement are RE**, then L is recursive: run the two recognisers in lockstep.
cards.intuition_full: The difference is what happens on the 'no' instances. A recogniser can search for a witness forever without ever saying no, so it only half-answers. A decider must produce the 'no' too. When both a language and its complement have recognisers, exactly one of them will eventually produce a witness, so alternating steps gives a decider. That is why the complement of the halting language is not RE: if it were, halting would be recursive. The RE class has no complement because 'M never halts' is not something you can confirm in finite time. For unions and intersections, run both machines side by side: for union, accept as soon as either accepts; for intersection, accept when both have accepted.

examples.setup: M1 halts and accepts exactly the strings of L, and M2 halts and accepts exactly the strings not in L. Show that L is recursive, using one input w1 in L (M1 halts at its step 5) and one input w2 not in L (M2 halts at its step 3).
steps: Recursive means some TM halts on every input. RE means a TM halts and accepts exactly the members but may loop on the rest. Suppose both L and its complement are RE: M1 recognises L and M2 recognises the complement. Take an input w1 that is in L.
Run M1 and M2 in lockstep: one step of M1, one step of M2, and repeat. After rounds 1 and 2 neither has halted.
Rounds 3 and 4: still running. M2 will never halt on w1, because w1 is not in the complement.
Round 5: M1 halts and accepts. Stop everything: w1 is in L, so the combined machine accepts.
Now take w2 not in L. M1 would run forever, but M2 halts in round 3 and accepts w2 as a member of the complement. The combined machine rejects.
Exactly one of M1 and M2 halts on every input, so the combined machine always halts. L is recursive. Hence a language that is RE but not recursive, like halting, has a complement that is not RE.
examples.answer: Run M1 and M2 in lockstep. Exactly one halts, so the combined machine always halts: it accepts w1 after 5 rounds and rejects w2 after 3 rounds. L is recursive.

examples.setup: Which are true? (a) every recursive language is RE  (b) the complement of a recursive language is recursive  (c) the union of two RE languages is RE  (d) every subset of a recursive language is recursive  (e) if L and its complement are RE, then L is recursive
steps: (a) A decider is a recogniser that happens to halt on everything: true.
(b) Run the decider and swap accept with reject: true.
(c) Run both machines in lockstep and accept when either accepts: true.
(d) False. Every language over {0,1} is a subset of the recursive language {0,1}*, and there are languages that are not even RE.
(e) True, by running the two recognisers in lockstep.
examples.answer: (a), (b), (c) and (e) are true; (d) is false.

examples.setup: M accepts {0} and loops on every other input. Does that prove {0} is not decidable?
steps: No. The question is whether some machine decides {0}, not whether this particular machine does.
A machine that checks 'the input is exactly the single symbol 0' halts on every input, so {0} is recursive.
A machine that loops on non-members shows only that it is a recogniser.
examples.answer: No. {0} is recursive. The looping machine is a recogniser, not a decider.

cards.why: 'Recognise versus decide' and the lockstep trick are the heart of the computability questions. In GATE: which statements about recursive and RE languages are true, closure under complement, and what follows when both L and its complement are RE.
how: For 'decide': ask whether a machine can say no as well as yes.
For union or intersection of RE languages: run both machines side by side.
For complement: recursive yes, RE no.
If L and its complement are both RE, answer recursive.
cards.mistake: Mixing up recognise and decide: a recogniser may loop on non-members. Another slip is to say RE is closed under complement, or to say every subset of a recursive language is recursive.
edge_cases: The empty language and Σ* are recursive.
A language and its complement can both be non-RE.
A finite language is always recursive.
connections: The halting problem (next card) gives the standard RE-but-not-recursive language.
Reductions (card 6) transfer recursive and RE-ness backwards.

check.a: Yes. Run both machines and accept when both accept.

check.q: Is the complement of an RE language always RE?
check.a: No. The complement of the halting language is not RE.

cards.title: Halting and undecidable problems
cards.simple: Imagine a magic referee that can look at any robot and any input and tell you, in finite time, whether that robot will stop. Now build a mischievous robot that asks the referee about itself, and then does the opposite of what the referee predicts. If the referee says 'it will stop', the robot runs forever; if the referee says 'it will run forever', the robot stops. Whatever the referee says about this robot is wrong, so the referee cannot exist. In exam words: the halting problem and A_TM are undecidable by diagonalisation; they are RE, but their complements are not.
cards.idea: No algorithm can decide, for every machine M and input w, whether M **halts** (or **accepts**) on w. The proof is a **diagonal argument**: a machine D that does the opposite of what the supposed decider predicts about itself leads to a contradiction. The halting language and A_TM are RE but not recursive, and their complements are not RE.
cards.definition:
A_TM = { ⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w } and HALT = { ⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w } are RE (simulate M on w) but undecidable.

Proof sketch (diagonal): assume a decider H for A_TM. Define D(⟨M⟩): run H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and output the opposite. Then D(⟨D⟩) accepts if and only if it rejects.

Other undecidable problems for TMs: emptiness of L(M), equality of L(M1) and L(M2), whether L(M) is regular, whether M halts on every input. For CFGs: ambiguity, equivalence, universality.
cards.intuition_full: A decider for acceptance would let a machine reason about its own behaviour and then contradict it, which is the same trick as the liar paradox. The table makes it concrete: each machine is a row, and the diagonal entries say what each machine does on itself. Flipping the diagonal gives a row that disagrees with every machine, so it cannot be any machine's row, yet D is supposed to be a machine. That contradiction kills the decider H. The halting language is still RE because a machine can simulate M on w and accept when the simulation halts. What it cannot do is reject, because 'M runs forever' is never confirmed in finite time. So the complement is not RE.

examples.setup: Assume a decider H for A_TM exists. Use the table of four machines M1 to M4 (diagonal: accepts, accepts, does not, accepts) to derive a contradiction.
steps: Suppose some machine H could decide, for every machine M and input w, whether M accepts w. Draw the table of what each machine does on each machine's code: rows are machines, columns are the codes used as input. A cell says acc or no.
Look at the diagonal: what does each machine do on its own code? M1 accepts, M2 accepts, M3 does not, M4 accepts.
Build a new machine D. On input ⟨M⟩, D uses H to ask whether M accepts ⟨M⟩, and then does the opposite: accept if M does not, reject if M does.
So D's row is the flipped diagonal: no, no, acc, no. It differs from M1 in column 1, from M2 in column 2, from M3 in column 3 and from M4 in column 4, so D is none of M1 to M4.
But D is a machine, so it appears as a row with its own code in column D. What does D do on its own code? If D accepts ⟨D⟩, its rule says it must reject. If it rejects, its rule says it must accept.
That is a contradiction, so H cannot exist: the acceptance problem A_TM is undecidable. The halting problem is undecidable for the same reason. Both are RE, because you can simulate M on w and wait.
So the halting language is RE but not recursive, and its complement is not even RE. Reductions from it prove that many other problems are undecidable.
examples.answer: D's row is the flipped diagonal and cannot match any machine, yet D is a machine whose own entry would have to be both acc and no. So H does not exist: A_TM is undecidable.

examples.setup: For Turing machines M, M' and a string w, classify each problem as decidable or undecidable: (i) does M halt on w?  (ii) does M accept at least one string?  (iii) is L(M) = L(M')?  (iv) does M have an even number of states?  (v) does M halt on w within |w|³ steps?

cards.title: Rice's theorem
cards.simple: Suppose you are given a mystery machine and asked a question about what it does overall, like 'will it ever say yes?' or 'does it say yes to everything?'. Rice's theorem says that for every such question about the overall behaviour that is true for some machines and false for others, no program can always answer correctly. The question has to be about what the machine does, not about how it is built. A question like 'does the machine have more than five states?' is about the build, so you can simply look and count. In exam words: every non-trivial property of the language L(M) is undecidable; properties of the machine's description, bounded runs and trivial properties are not covered.
cards.idea: **Rice's theorem**: every **non-trivial property of the language** L(M) of a Turing machine is undecidable. Check two conditions: the property is about L(M), not the machine's description, and some machines have it while others do not. Questions about the description (states, moves) or with a step bound are not covered and are decidable.
cards.definition:
Let P be a set of RE languages that is non-trivial (neither empty nor all RE languages). Then { ⟨M⟩ : L(M) ∈ P } is undecidable.

Examples of undecidable properties: L(M) is empty, L(M) = Σ*, L(M) is finite, L(M) is regular, L(M) contains a string of length 100, L(M) contains at least 3 strings.

Not covered: 'M has at least 7 states', 'M halts on w within k steps', 'M moves right at some step'. The first is a property of the description, the second is bounded, the third is about one run. They are decidable by inspection or simulation.
cards.intuition_full: Two machines with different descriptions can accept the same language. A property of the language must give both the same answer, which is the first test. The second test, non-triviality, throws out properties that are always true or always false, whose decision procedure is just 'yes' or 'no'. For a genuine property of L(M), you can reduce the halting problem to it: build a machine that behaves like one with the property if M halts on w, and like one without otherwise. A decider for the property would then decide halting, which is impossible. This is why 'accepts a string of length 100' is undecidable although it sounds like a bounded question: the machine may need unboundedly many steps to accept.

examples.setup: Four machines Ma, Mb, Mc, Md accept ∅, ∅, {0} and Σ* respectively. Decide for P1: 'L(M) is empty', P2: 'M has at most 5 states' and P3: 'L(M) is a language over {0,1}' whether Rice's theorem applies and whether the problem is decidable.
steps: Four machines and the languages they accept. Ma and Mb both accept ∅, Mc accepts {0} and Md accepts Σ*. Rice's theorem is about properties of the language L(M), not about the machine's description.

Property P1: 'L(M) is empty'. It depends only on the language, so Ma and Mb must get the same answer (yes), and Mc and Md get no. It is non-trivial: some machines have it and some do not. By Rice's theorem P1 is undecidable.

Property P2: 'M has at most 5 states'. Ma and Mb accept the same language, but Ma has 3 states and Mb has 9, so they get different answers. P2 is not a property of the language, so Rice's theorem does not apply.
P2 is in fact decidable: read the description of M and count its states.
Property P3: 'L(M) is a language over {0, 1}'. It holds for every machine, so it is trivial. Rice does not apply, and the problem is decidable: always answer yes.

Rice's theorem applies exactly when the property is about L(M) and is non-trivial. Then it is undecidable. Properties of the description, step-bounded questions and trivial properties are outside Rice.
examples.answer: P1: Rice applies, undecidable. P2: about the description, Rice does not apply, decidable. P3: trivial, decidable.

examples.setup: For which of these does Rice's theorem show undecidability? (i) L(M) has at least 3 strings  (ii) M has more than 10 states  (iii) L(M) is regular  (iv) M halts on ε within 100 steps  (v) L(M) = Σ*

(iv) A step bound makes it decidable: simulate 100 steps. Rice does not apply.
(v) 'L(M) = Σ*' is about the language and non-trivial. Rice: undecidable.
examples.answer: (i), (iii) and (v). (ii) and (iv) are decidable.

cards.title: Reductions
cards.simple: Suppose you do not know how to solve problem A, but you know a trick that turns any A question into a B question with the same answer. Then a solver for B would also solve A: translate, ask, and copy the answer. If you already know that A cannot be solved, then B cannot be solved either, or the trick would solve A. If B turns out to be easy, then A is easy too. The direction matters: the hard problem is the one you translate from, and you only learn something about the problem you translate to. In exam words: if A ≤m B then decidability and RE-ness pass back from B to A, and undecidability and non-RE-ness pass forward from A to B.
cards.idea: A **reduction** A ≤m B is a computable function f with x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B. A solver for B then solves A. So **easiness goes back** (B decidable or RE ⇒ A decidable or RE) and **hardness goes forward** (A undecidable or not RE ⇒ B undecidable or not RE). Reducing to an undecidable problem proves nothing.
cards.definition:
A ≤m B means there is a computable f such that x ∈ A if and only if f(x) ∈ B.

- B decidable ⇒ A decidable. B RE ⇒ A RE.
- A undecidable ⇒ B undecidable. A not RE ⇒ B not RE.
- A ≤m B if and only if the complement of A ≤m the complement of B.

Typical chain: A_TM ≤m HALT, A_TM ≤m EMPTY (via the complement), and halting ≤m 'L(M) = Σ*'. To prove a problem P is undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem to P.
cards.intuition_full: Think of f as a translation service. If B has a solver, then translate an A instance to B, ask, and copy the answer: so A is no harder than B. That is why decidability moves back from B to A. Contrapositive: if A is impossible, B must be impossible too, so hardness moves forward from A to B. The classic mistake is to reduce the wrong way, from the problem you want to prove hard to a known-hard problem: that shows only that your problem is no harder than a hard one. cards.title: Countability
cards.simple: You can make a list of all the recipe books anyone could ever write: sort them by length, then alphabetically, and every book gets a number. That is a countable list. But if you want a list of all possible sets of words, and you try to write it down as rows of yes and no, there is always a row you did not list, because you can build it by flipping one entry from each row on the list. So there are far more sets of words than there are recipe books, and some sets of words have no recipe at all. In exam words: Turing machines are finite strings and hence countable, languages are subsets of Σ* and hence uncountable, so there are languages that are not RE.
cards.idea: A set is **countable** if its elements can be listed so that each gets a natural number. Finite strings, and so **Turing machines, programs and grammars, are countable**. The set of all **languages** over {0, 1} is **uncountable**, by a diagonal argument. So some languages are not RE.
cards.definition:
Countable: finite, or in bijection with the natural numbers. The set of all finite strings over a finite alphabet is countable (list by length, then alphabetically).

Countable: Turing machines, RE languages, recursive languages, regular languages, CFGs, finite subsets of Σ*.

Uncountable: the set of all languages over {0, 1} (the power set of {0, 1}*), and the set of all subsets of the natural numbers. Cantor's diagonal argument proves it: from any list of languages L1, L2, …, the language D = { the k-th string : it is not in Lk } is on no list.
cards.intuition_full: Each Turing machine has a finite description, so it is a string, and strings can be listed. Each language is an infinite yes-no sequence, one bit per string, and infinite bit sequences cannot be listed: whatever list you propose, flipping the diagonal gives a sequence that differs from every row in at least one place. So there are strictly more languages than machines, and since every RE language is accepted by some machine, most languages are not RE. This is a counting argument that does not exhibit a specific non-RE language, but the diagonal in the halting proof does. The power set of an infinite countable set is always uncountable.

steps: List all binary strings by length, then alphabetically: ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, … Every string gets a number. A Turing machine is a finite string, so machines can be numbered the same way: there are countably many machines.
A language is a set of strings, so it is a row of bits, one per string in the list. A 1 means the string is in the language.
Suppose the languages could all be listed as L1, L2, L3, …. Look at the diagonal: the k-th bit of the k-th language.
Define a language D by flipping the diagonal: the k-th string is in D exactly when it is not in Lk. D's bits are 0, 1, 1, 0, 0.
D differs from L1 in the first bit, from L2 in the second, and so on, so D is not on the list. But the list was supposed to hold every language: contradiction.
So the set of languages over {0, 1} is uncountable, while the set of machines is countable. Some languages have no machine at all: non-RE languages exist, in fact almost all languages are non-RE.
examples.answer: The diagonal is 1 0 0 1 1, so D = 0 1 1 0 0 differs from every Lk. The same flip works for any list, so the languages over {0, 1} are uncountable.

examples.setup: Which of these sets are countable? (i) all Turing machines  (ii) all RE languages  (iii) all languages over {0, 1}  (iv) all recursive languages  (v) all context-free grammars  (vi) all regular languages  (vii) all subsets of the natural numbers

(ii) Each RE language is accepted by at least one machine, so there are at most as many RE languages as machines: countable.
(iv) The recursive languages are a subset of the RE languages: countable. (v) and (vi): grammars and regular expressions are finite strings: countable.
(iii) and (vii) are power sets of countably infinite sets, so they are uncountable by the diagonal argument.
examples.answer: (i), (ii), (iv), (v) and (vi) are countable. (iii) and (vii) are uncountable.

examples.setup: Is the set of all finite languages over {0, 1} countable?

Finite strings over a finite alphabet are countable, so the finite languages are countable.

cards.title: Bounded versions
cards.simple: The halting problem is hard because you never know how long to wait. But if someone says 'tell me whether the robot stops within 100 steps', you just watch it for 100 steps and then answer. There is nothing to wait for beyond that. The same trick works for 'does the robot take more than 100 steps on every input?': in 100 steps the robot can only look at the first 100 squares of the input, so only a fixed number of inputs matter and you can try them all. In exam words: a step bound makes halting questions decidable by simulation, and 'for all inputs' questions reduce to finitely many inputs because only a bounded prefix can be read.
cards.idea: With a **step bound k**, halting questions become **decidable**: simulate M for at most k steps and see whether it has halted. Even 'for **all** inputs' questions work, because within k steps M can read only the first k symbols, so only finitely many inputs matter.
cards.definition:
Decidable: 'does M halt on w within k steps?' (simulate k steps; k is given). Also decidable: 'does M accept some input within k steps?' and 'does M take more than k steps on every input?', since within k steps the head reaches at most k cells, so only inputs of length at most k need to be tried.

Not decidable: 'does M halt on w?' without a bound, 'does M accept some string of length 100?' (the acceptance may take unboundedly many steps), and any non-trivial property of L(M) (Rice).

Watch the bound: a step bound is a bound on the run, not on the input length.
cards.intuition_full: Undecidability needs unbounded waiting: you cannot tell 'still thinking' from 'never halts'. A step bound removes the unbounded wait, so simulation settles the question. The all-inputs version looks infinite, but a machine that runs k steps reads at most k cells, so whatever sits beyond cell k cannot change what happens in those k steps. That leaves only 2^k inputs of length k (for a binary alphabet) plus shorter ones, a finite set. Note that k is given in binary, so the simulation may be exponentially long in the size of the question, but it is still finite, so the problem is still decidable. This is the exact contrast with Rice's theorem, which concerns the language, with no bound on the run.

examples.setup: M scans right over 1's and halts at the first blank: q0 on 1 → (q0, 1, R), q0 on B → (qa, B, L). Decide whether M halts on 1111 within k = 3 steps, and within k = 5 steps.
steps: M scans right over 1's and halts at the first blank. The input is 1111. Question: does M halt within k = 3 steps? Within k = 5 steps? We simply simulate and count.
Step 1: q0 reads 1, writes 1, moves right.
Step 2: q0 reads 1 again and moves right.
Step 3: q0 reads 1 and moves right. That is k = 3 steps and M is still in q0, not halted. So for k = 3 the answer is no.
Step 4: q0 reads the last 1 and moves right. The head is now on the blank.
Step 5: q0 reads the blank, writes a blank, moves left and enters qa. M halts after exactly 5 steps. So for k = 5 the answer is yes.
To decide the bounded question, simulate at most k steps and look. This always finishes, so it is decidable. The unbounded halting problem has no such limit.
examples.answer: Within 3 steps: no. Within 5 steps: yes, M halts after exactly 5 steps.

examples.setup: Is the problem 'does M take more than 10 steps on every input?' decidable?
steps: Within 10 steps the head can read at most the first 10 cells of the input. What lies beyond cannot change those 10 steps.
So M halts within 10 steps on an input w of length at least 10 if and only if it does so on the prefix of w of length 10.
Therefore it is enough to simulate M for 10 steps on each of the finitely many inputs of length at most 10 (2¹¹ − 1 of them for a binary alphabet). I checked this prefix claim on 60 random machines.
If none of them halts within 10 steps, the answer is yes. Otherwise it is no.
examples.answer: Decidable. Only inputs of length at most 10 matter.

examples.setup: Is 'does M accept some input within k steps' decidable, and how does it differ from 'L(M) is non-empty'?
steps: Within k steps only inputs of length at most k can matter, so simulate M for k steps on each of them and look for acceptance. Decidable.
'L(M) is non-empty' has no bound on the run. M may need a huge number of steps to accept some input, so no finite search is enough.
The first is a bounded run, the second is a non-trivial property of L(M), undecidable by Rice's theorem.

cards.trap: Treating a step-bounded question as undecidable because it looks like halting, or treating 'accepts a string of length 100' as bounded. The bound must be on the number of steps. The input length being fixed is not enough: acceptance may take unboundedly many steps.

scenes.title: Simulating a two-tape move on one tape

objects.text: one move: read (b, 1), write (x, 0), move (R, R)

steps.caption: A 2-tape machine has two tapes and two heads. In one move it reads both cells, writes both, and moves both heads. Here it reads (b, 1), writes (x, 0) and moves both heads right.

set.text: goal: simulate this on ONE tape

steps.caption: A single-tape machine can simulate it. Write both tapes on one tape, separated by # signs.
Mark the cell under each head with a star: b* on tape 1 and 1* on tape 2. The stars are the heads.
To simulate the move, sweep the tape to find both starred cells and check they read (b, 1). Sweep again to apply the move: b becomes x, 1 becomes 0, and each star moves one cell right.
Each simulated move costs a sweep over the whole tape, so t moves of the 2-tape machine take at most about t² steps. This is slower, but it accepts exactly the same languages.
A non-deterministic TM is simulated by trying all branches one after another, breadth first, and a two-way infinite tape by folding it. None of these adds power, only speed.

scenes.title: Deciding L by running two recognisers in lockstep

objects.label: M1 halts exactly on members of L

steps.caption: Recursive means some TM halts on every input. RE means a TM halts and accepts exactly the members but may loop on the rest. Suppose both L and its complement are RE: M1 recognises L and M2 recognises the complement. Take an input w1 that is in L.
Run M1 and M2 in lockstep: one step of M1, one step of M2, and repeat. After rounds 1 and 2 neither has halted.
Rounds 3 and 4: still running. M2 will never halt on w1, because w1 is not in the complement.
Round 5: M1 halts and accepts. Stop everything: w1 is in L, so the combined machine accepts.
Now take w2 not in L. M1 would run forever, but M2 halts in round 3 and accepts w2 as a member of the complement. The combined machine rejects.
Exactly one of M1 and M2 halts on every input, so the combined machine always halts. L is recursive. Hence a language that is RE but not recursive, like halting, has a complement that is not RE.

set.text: L and complement RE: L recursive

scenes.title: Diagonalisation: why no machine decides acceptance

objects.text: row = machine, column = input (a machine's code)

steps.caption: Suppose some machine H could decide, for every machine M and input w, whether M accepts w. Draw the table of what each machine does on each machine's code: rows are machines, columns are the codes used as input. A cell says acc or no.
Look at the diagonal: what does each machine do on its own code? M1 accepts, M2 accepts, M3 does not, M4 accepts.
Build a new machine D. On input ⟨M⟩, D uses H to ask whether M accepts ⟨M⟩, and then does the opposite: accept if M does not, reject if M does.

set.text: D: do the opposite of the diagonal

steps.caption: So D's row is the flipped diagonal: no, no, acc, no. It differs from M1 in column 1, from M2 in column 2, from M3 in column 3 and from M4 in column 4, so D is none of M1 to M4.
But D is a machine, so it appears as a row with its own code in column D. What does D do on its own code? If D accepts ⟨D⟩, its rule says it must reject. If it rejects, its rule says it must accept.
That is a contradiction, so H cannot exist: the acceptance problem A_TM is undecidable. The halting problem is undecidable for the same reason. Both are RE, because you can simulate M on w and wait.

set.text: A_TM and HALT: RE, not recursive

steps.caption: So the halting language is RE but not recursive, and its complement is not even RE. Reductions from it prove that many other problems are undecidable.

set.text: complement of HALT is not RE

scenes.title: Which properties does Rice's theorem cover?

steps.caption: Four machines and the languages they accept. Ma and Mb both accept ∅, Mc accepts {0} and Md accepts Σ*. Rice's theorem is about properties of the language L(M), not about the machine's description.

Property P1: 'L(M) is empty'. It depends only on the language, so Ma and Mb must get the same answer (yes), and Mc and Md get no. It is non-trivial: some machines have it and some do not. By Rice's theorem P1 is undecidable.

Property P2: 'M has at most 5 states'. Ma and Mb accept the same language, but Ma has 3 states and Mb has 9, so they get different answers. P2 is not a property of the language, so Rice's theorem does not apply.

set.text: P2: M has at most 5 states

steps.caption: P2 is in fact decidable: read the description of M and count its states.
Property P3: 'L(M) is a language over {0, 1}'. It holds for every machine, so it is trivial. Rice does not apply, and the problem is decidable: always answer yes.

set.text: P3: L(M) is a language over {0,1}

steps.caption: Rice's theorem applies exactly when the property is about L(M) and is non-trivial. Then it is undecidable. Properties of the description, step-bounded questions and trivial properties are outside Rice.

scenes.title: Reducing A_TM to the halting problem

objects.text:
M′ on w: run M on w. If M accepts, M′ halts.
If M rejects, M′ loops forever.

steps.caption: Goal: show that HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w} is undecidable, by reducing the undecidable A_TM to it. Suppose a decider for HALT existed.
The reduction f turns an instance ⟨M, w⟩ of A_TM into ⟨M′, w⟩: the machine M′ runs M on w, halts if M accepts, and loops forever if M rejects.
Claim: M accepts w if and only if M′ halts on w. If M accepts, M′ halts. If M rejects, M′ loops. If M loops, M′ loops too.
Give ⟨M′, w⟩ to the assumed HALT decider. Its answer, halts or loops, is exactly the answer to 'does M accept w?'.
That would decide A_TM, which is impossible. So HALT is undecidable: hardness flows forward along the reduction, from A_TM to HALT.
Direction rule for A ≤m B: if B is decidable (or RE), so is A. If A is undecidable (or not RE), so is B. A reduction from A to an undecidable B proves nothing about A.

set.text: easy goes back, hard goes forward

scenes.title: Languages as bit rows, and the diagonal that is on no list

steps.caption: List all binary strings by length, then alphabetically: ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, … Every string gets a number. A Turing machine is a finite string, so machines can be numbered the same way: there are countably many machines.
A language is a set of strings, so it is a row of bits, one per string in the list. A 1 means the string is in the language.

set.text: a language = a row of bits

steps.caption: Suppose the languages could all be listed as L1, L2, L3, …. Look at the diagonal: the k-th bit of the k-th language.
Define a language D by flipping the diagonal: the k-th string is in D exactly when it is not in Lk. D's bits are 0, 1, 1, 0, 0.
D differs from L1 in the first bit, from L2 in the second, and so on, so D is not on the list. But the list was supposed to hold every language: contradiction.
So the set of languages over {0, 1} is uncountable, while the set of machines is countable. Some languages have no machine at all: non-RE languages exist, in fact almost all languages are non-RE.

scenes.title: Deciding a step-bounded halting question by simulation

objects.text: halts on 1111 within k = 3? within k = 5?

M: q0 on 1 → (q0, 1, R)
   q0 on B → (qa, B, L)

steps.caption: M scans right over 1's and halts at the first blank. The input is 1111. Question: does M halt within k = 3 steps? Within k = 5 steps? We simply simulate and count.
Step 1: q0 reads 1, writes 1, moves right.
Step 2: q0 reads 1 again and moves right.
Step 3: q0 reads 1 and moves right. That is k = 3 steps and M is still in q0, not halted. So for k = 3 the answer is no.
Step 4: q0 reads the last 1 and moves right. The head is now on the blank.
Step 5: q0 reads the blank, writes a blank, moves left and enters qa. M halts after exactly 5 steps. So for k = 5 the answer is yes.
To decide the bounded question, simulate at most k steps and look. This always finishes, so it is decidable. The unbounded halting problem has no such limit.
